title: Strengthened bounds for the probability of k-out-of-n events
contribution: Re-derives the Prekopa-Gao partially aggregated LP (PAM) as a relaxation of the exponential Boolean LP and strengthens it by projecting out the dropped variables, giving inequalities (SPAM) that raise lower bounds on P(at least k of n events) and, on worst-case distributions found with BARON, reach the exact Boolean-model bound.
problem_entry: With moments only up to level m < n, P(mu >= k) can only be bounded; enters from the known PAM LP and asks what inequalities can be appended to it (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: PAM = Boolean LP after row duplication/aggregation with the w_C variables dropped; instead project w_C out (it is absent from the objective) and add the projection inequalities (15)-(16) (pp. 3-7).
assumptions: Bernoulli events with known joint probabilities p_S for |S| <= m; projection stated per layer i with special cases i = n-1, n (pp. 2, 5).
proof_devices: Dimension of the 0-1 slice {sum x = i} by n explicit linearly independent vectors (Lemma 1), p. 5
Projection via Farkas' lemma: list extreme rays of {u: u^T G >= 0}, certify extremality by counting tight columns, exclude other rays by a coordinate-swap contradiction (Prop. 2), pp. 6-7
Worst-case-distribution model: dualise the inner LPs into one max problem over p_S and solve with BARON (Appendix 2), pp. 12-13
experiments: Prekopa-Gao's three 20-event examples, k = 1 and k = 3 lower bounds vs FAM, PAM, PAM(3) (Tables 4-5, p. 9); upper bounds not improved (p. 10); BARON-found worst-case distributions for n = 10, m = 3, k = 2-4 where SPAM equals the Boolean bound (Table 6, p. 10).
positioning: Builds directly on Prekopa-Gao [9] and the binomial-moment LP line (Prekopa, Boros); critique of earlier work is that aggregation loses individual information (p. 2).
writing: Short note; one-sentence 'key contribution' statement in the introduction (p. 2); no conclusion section; table labels inconsistent with text (Examples 4-6 vs 1-3, pp. 8-9).
limits_future: No improvement in upper bounds (p. 10); in Table 5 Example 1 SPAM is below three-moment PAM(3) (p. 9); no future-work section.

method_links.note: Cheap LP bound strengthened with inequalities derived from the structure of the aggregation (projection).
Exact exponential Boolean LP used as ceiling against which SPAM is judged on worst-case distributions.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: optimise the instance to maximise the gap between two relaxations
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Distributions maximising SPAM - PAM found by dualising inner LPs and solving the resulting max problem with BARON.

transferable: To show where a new inequality family matters, write max over data of (new bound - old bound), dualise the inner LP into a single nonconvex max problem and solve it with a global solver (pp. 10, 12-13).
Project out an exponential block by computing the extreme rays of {u: u^T G >= 0} via Farkas, certifying extremality by tight-column counts (pp. 6-7).

quotes.text: Our key contribution is to identify inequalities that can be appended to PAM to strengthen the bounds.
However, we do not observe improvement in the new upper bounds.

title: On a cardinality-constrained transportation problem with market choice
contribution: Proves that for the transportation problem with market choice with demands in {1,2}, intersecting the convex hull with a cardinality constraint on rejected markets keeps it integral, generalising the matching-cardinality result and giving polynomial solvability; a demand of 3 breaks it.
problem_entry: Generalise the classical integrality of matching polytope plus cardinality constraint to simple TPMC (d_j <= 2), motivated by a service-level constraint (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Avoid the perfect-matching reduction (cardinality on an edge subset breaks integrality, Example 1) and prove the edge property: optimal solutions of intermediate cardinality always exist (pp. 3-5).
assumptions: Integral data, d_j <= 2; supplies reduced to 1 by node splitting, polynomial since s_i <= 2|V2| (pp. 3, 5).
proof_devices: Edge-property lemma: edge property implies cardinality-constrained hull = hull cut by constraint (Prop. 2, credited to [2]), pp. 4-5
Claim 1: construct two solutions with values rho - delta and rho + delta, p. 5
Bipartite conflict graph of full and partial nodes, p. 6
Path-marking Algorithm 1 with induction-on-iterations correctness proof (Claims 9-11), pp. 11-13
positioning: Generalises Nemhauser-Trotter-type matching-cardinality integrality [8]; builds on the TPMC introduction [4] and an edge-property technique from [2] (pp. 1-4).
writing: Short note: single main theorem stated in §1.3 with corollaries and two examples before the proof (pp. 3-4); no conclusion section.
limits_future: Fails with a demand of 3 (Example 2, p. 4); complexity of min-weight perfect matching with a cardinality constraint on an edge subset stated open (p. 3). Version read is arXiv v1 without M. Walter.

method_links.note: Hypothesis d_j <= 2 dropped and fractional vertex exhibited; Example 1 shows why the matching-polytope route fails.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: pick the proof route by first testing it on a counterexample
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Generic matching-polytope approach judged less fruitful because Example 1 shows the analogous statement fails there.

transferable: To show one cardinality constraint keeps a hull integral, prove the edge property (optimal solutions of intermediate cardinality) instead of integrality directly (pp. 4-5).
Before routing a proof through a known polytope, check whether the target statement already fails for that polytope (Example 1, p. 3).
coauthors: Pelin Damci-Kurt, Simge Kucukyavuz (arXiv v1); M. Walter on published version (metadata only)

quotes.text: Therefore a generic approach considering the perfect matching polytope appears to be less fruitful.
The next example illustrates that the statement of Theorem 1 does not hold in such case.

title: Groves mechanisms and communication externalities
contribution: In a two-platform communication model with externalities, gives a polynomial algorithm for the efficient adoption pattern, proves no individually rational and feasible Groves mechanism exists, characterises the minimal-deficit mechanism and, for two agents, the unique second-best-efficient feasible Groves mechanism.
problem_entry: Economics question (efficient platform adoption and its implementation) where the efficiency step is a 0-1 optimisation problem P(e) (pp. 2, 6).
key_idea: Monotonicity (higher theta adopts first) and necessary optimality conditions prune 2^N candidates to a chain, giving about |N_alpha||N_beta| operations; then mechanism-design impossibility and characterisations (pp. 6-10, 14, 20).
assumptions: Two platforms, linear communicative benefit, platform-specific costs, quasi-linear utility; assumptions chosen to intensify the externality (pp. 4-6).
proof_devices: Exchange argument for monotonicity (Lemma 1), p. 6
Two-agent counterexample economy for impossibility (Prop. 2), pp. 10-11
Single-valuation transfer perturbation for necessity of Condition A (Prop. 4), pp. 18-19
experiments: none (worked numerical economy tracing the algorithm, pp. 8-9)
positioning: Contrasts with Groves literature on public and private goods; Pivotal mechanism fails feasibility here; deficit judged per economy, not worst case or asymptotically (p. 3).
writing: Economics style: motivating anecdotes (rail gauges, language learning), axioms section, propositions with proofs deferred to appendices (pp. 2-4, 9).
limits_future: Second-best result only for two agents because a general result is out of reach (p. 20); surplus question open (p. 11); non-Groves mechanisms left for future work (pp. 21-22); more-than-two-platform NP-completeness asserted with proof 'available on request' (p. 7).

method_links.note: Impossibility paired with achievability of any three axioms and a sufficient condition for deficit; outside the MINLP field.

transferable: Prove a monotonicity lemma to collapse a 2^N assignment search into a short threshold chain (Lemma 1, Table 1, pp. 6-8).

quotes.text: We first provide an algorithm that determines the efficient outcome.
The combinatorial nature of the problem makes this very difficult to ascertain.

title: Closedness of integer hulls of simple conic sets
contribution: Characterises completely when the integer hull of a simple conic mixed-integer set is closed, gives a polynomial-time check for poly-checkable cones, proves the Lorentz cone is poly-checkable, and shows closedness survives finite intersection in the pure integer case but not the mixed-integer case.
problem_entry: Meyer's theorem (integer hull of a rational polyhedron is a rational polyhedron) has no conic analogue, so ask the more basic question whether the conic integer hull is closed (p. 1).
key_idea: Map the set by T(x,y) = Ax + By - b, trading a complicated set for a simple one (C intersect V) and a translated mixed-integer lattice; closedness then depends on four checkable cases (pp. 2, 4-5).
assumptions: Rational data; C full-dimensional, pointed, closed, generated by a strictly convex set; intersection result pure integer with lineality space generated by integer points (pp. 2-3).
proof_devices: Affine map that preserves closedness, moving difficulty from set to lattice (Prop. 2), pp. 4-5
Generalisation of the authors' pure-integer closedness results to mixed-integer lattices, p. 2
Dirichlet approximation for the irrational-ray counterexample (Example 1), p. 4
Hermite normal form plus perfect-square test for the Lorentz cone, pp. 3, 23
positioning: Extends the authors' own pure-integer closedness paper [4] and an extended abstract [5]; framed against Meyer's MILP theorem (pp. 1-2, 4).
writing: Main results section with all theorems before proofs (§2, pp. 2-4); proof sketch section before details (§3.1, p. 4); mild enthusiasm ('We find it interesting', p. 1).
limits_future: Intersection theorem fails for mixed-integer sets (Example 1, p. 4); rational-data mixed-integer version left open (p. 4).

method_links.note: Start from the MILP structure theorem (Meyer) and ask the weakest meaningful analogue for conic sets.
Positive intersection theorem paired with a mixed-integer counterexample and an explicitly open case.

transferable: When the MILP analogue of a structure theorem fails for a nonlinear class, step down to a weaker property (closedness) and characterise it completely (p. 1).
Move complexity from the set into the lattice by an affine map after proving the map preserves the property (pp. 4-5).
Turn an existence condition into an algorithm by isolating one number-theoretic test for the specific cone (p. 3).

quotes.text: We find it interesting that it is possible to construct an algorithm (let alone one that runs in polynomial-time) to test the closedness of integer hulls of unbounded nonlinear sets.
We have not been able to resolve this question.

title: Some cut-generating functions for second-order conic sets
contribution: Shows that for bounded conic sets linear-IP cut-generating functions composed with conic aggregations give the integer hull, introduces the first closed-form family of subadditive second-order-cone-nondecreasing functions, and proves the two families together give the integer hull of intersections of conic sections in R^2.
problem_entry: Conic subadditive duality exists, but far less is known than for linear IP (CG characterisation, 2n-row sufficiency, finite lists); aim to understand which subsets of F_K suffice (p. 2).
key_idea: Bounded cut-off region implies the cut comes from one rational polyhedral outer approximation with p <= 2^n aggregations; the hyperbola branch shows unbounded cases need new functions f_gamma, which obtain x1 >= 1 in one step where conic CG and conic MIR fail (pp. 2-6).
assumptions: Regular cone K, nonempty interior; B bounded for Theorem 1; R^2, non-degenerate hyperbolas in Lemma 1 form, non-redundant constraints for Theorem 3 (pp. 2, 5-6).
proof_devices: Conic strong duality to obtain y in K* aggregations (Lemma 4), p. 6
Rational separating hyperplane by perturbation with interior points of the dual recession cone (Lemma 5), pp. 6-7
B bounded iff pi in interior of dual recession cone (Prop. 2), p. 7
Counterexamples: every polyhedral outer approximation of x1 x2 >= 1 contains (0,k) (Prop. 3), p. 8; f_gamma not orthant-nondecreasing (Remark 1), p. 5
positioning: Generalises linear IP subadditive duality results; compares with split-disjunctive conic cuts, conic CG [28] and conic MIR [29], showing the latter two cannot produce the hyperbola cuts (pp. 2-4).
writing: All results in §2 with motivating hyperbola example before the new family (pp. 3-4); hedged scope ('under some minor technical conditions', abstract).
limits_future: Completeness only in R^2 and for second-order cone; no conclusion or future-work section (p. 6).

method_links.note: The MILP list (subadditive duality, CG characterisation, finite function lists) is the template; asks the same of conic IP.
Theorem 1 paired with Prop. 3 showing failure without boundedness; Remark 1 bounds the new family.
Substructure is a single conic section in R^2, not a multi-constraint set.

transferable: Use the smallest unbounded example to show a finite polyhedral-outer-approximation argument cannot work, then design the new object to close exactly that example (pp. 3-4).
Make a separating hyperplane rational by perturbing with a positive combination of affinely independent interior points of the dual recession cone (Lemma 5, pp. 6-7).

quotes.text: However, it would be much nicer if we could directly obtain x1 ≥ 1 without resorting to obtaining it as an implication of an infinite sequence of cuts.
Geometrically, Theorem 1 can be interpreted as the fact that if the set of points separated is bounded, then the cut can be obtained using a rational polyhedral outer approximation.

title: Sparse principal component analysis and its ℓ1-relaxation
contribution: Proves, with no assumption on the data, that the l1-relaxation of sparse PCA (and of any semi-norm maximisation) is within a factor 2.95 of the l0 optimum for k >= 15 via analysis of a randomized rounding, and constructs an instance with ratio 1.32.
problem_entry: The popular practice of replacing the l0 constraint by an l1 constraint in SPCA had no theory comparing the two optimal values (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Analyse unbiased randomized rounding of the l1 solution; control the upper tail of a non-Lipschitz semi-norm through l0 and l2 norms of the rounded vector, which concentrate (pp. 4-5).
assumptions: None on the data (any PSD A or semi-norm phi); k >= 15 (pp. 3-4).
proof_devices: Jensen on unbiased rounding for expected value, p. 5
Bound phi via support size and l2 norm (Lemma 5) and integrate over tails, p. 5
Conditional layer-cake decomposition (Lemma 2), p. 6
Concentration for l0 and l2 norms of the rounded vector, pp. 7-9
Worst-case instance: rank-one A reduced to a four-variable problem (16), solved by discretisation and certified by an explicit feasible point, pp. 12-14
experiments: Only 'limited computational experiments' showing ratios well below 1.32 (p. 5); Figure 2 plots the discretised worst-case ratio vs k (p. 14).
positioning: Contrasts with sparse-regression l0-l1 equivalences that need RIP or irrepresentable conditions; builds on the rounding of [11], adding use of positive semidefiniteness (p. 3).
writing: Main results section with a paragraph-long high-level proof idea before the proof (pp. 4-5); 'to the best of our knowledge, the first' claim (abstract).
limits_future: Gap between 1.32 and 2.95 open, speculation that 1.32 is closer (p. 5); constants improve for larger k (p. 4); parameter values in Theorem 1 (gamma 0.4051, g 2.996, p. 4) differ from those in §3.6 (0.44, 2.69, p. 11), not reconciled in the text read.

method_links.note: A widespread practice (l1 surrogate) given its first theorem with a data-independent ratio measure.
Upper bound 2.95 with constructed lower bound 1.32; gap stated open.
l1 problem as a bound on the l0 optimum, turned into a feasible solution with constant guarantee by rounding (weak link).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: optimise the instance to maximise the gap between two relaxations
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Worst-case l1/l0 ratio found by solving a reduced optimisation problem over rank-one instances.

transferable: When a non-Lipschitz objective does not concentrate, bound it by quantities that do (support size, norm) and integrate over their tails (p. 5).
For a lower bound on a worst-case ratio, restrict to a structured family, reduce to a few aggregate variables, solve numerically, then certify with one explicit feasible point (pp. 12-14).
coauthors: Rahul Mazumder, Marco Molinaro, Guanyi Wang

quotes.text: In this paper, we prove that, independent of the data, the optimal objective function value of the problem with ℓ0 constraint is within a constant factor of the the optimal objective function value of the problem with ℓ1 constraint.
In our limited computational experiments, we saw ratios significantly lesser than 1.32, so we speculate that the lower bound of 1.32 is perhaps closer to the actual constant.

title: Aggregation-based cutting-planes for packing and covering integer programs
contribution: Proves that for packing and covering (with bounds) IPs the CG and aggregation closures are tightly 2-approximated by their 1-row versions, that this fails arbitrarily for general IPs, and that k-aggregation closure rank grows at least logarithmically in the integrality gap, with experiments on random and market-split instances.
problem_entry: Aggregation cuts underlie many key solver cut families but lacked theory; ask when aggregation helps and where it is limited (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Sandwich closures via a pre-processed LP (zeroing infeasible columns for packing; knapsack-cover LP for covering with bounds) and use the containment form of approximation, which survives infinite intersections (pp. 4-8).
assumptions: Nonnegative rational data; bounds for covering; A_ij <= b_i for rank bounds; extends to infinitely many inequalities (pp. 2, 5-6).
proof_devices: alpha-approximation iff U contained in alpha V, preserved under intersections (Prop. 1), p. 8
Pre-processed LP as intermediate relaxation, with proof-map diagrams marking tight examples and unbounded ratios (Figures 1-2), pp. 5-6
KC-LP route shown to fail for covering CG closure (L z^C <= z^KC), forcing a separate proof, p. 6
Rank lower bound from integrality gap (Theorems 3, 5), pp. 5-6, 11-12
experiments: Exact CG closures with CPLEX 12.6: random equality IPs n = 10-16 with planted binary solution, instances with gap <= 2 discarded, mean z^1C/z^C 11.46-15.16; 100 market-split instances where the 1-row CG closure misses infeasibility in 50 of 90 infeasible cases (pp. 7-8).
positioning: Notes empirical study of aggregation cuts [11] but no theory; adds to few results relating integrality gap to rank [22, 27] (pp. 2, 5).
writing: All results with proof-map figures in §2 before proofs; explicit 'From cut selection perspective, the insight here is' takeaway in the introduction (p. 2); separate open-questions section (p. 8).
limits_future: Open: is the aggregation closure a polyhedron (only dense A shown); can multipliers be restricted by sign pattern for general IPs (p. 8).

method_links.note: Ubiquitous solver cut practice turned into a closure-comparison theorem with data-independent factor and read back as cut-selection advice.
Tight factor 2, negative class (general IPs), and a failing proof route made explicit.
Exact CG closure computed as ceiling on small instances, exclusions written into the generator.

transferable: Compare closures defined by infinitely many cuts through the containment form U contained in alpha V, which survives arbitrary intersections (Prop. 1, p. 8).
Draw the proof as a diagram of <= relations between named relaxation values, marking tight examples and unbounded ratios (Figures 1-2, pp. 5-6).
Pair a positive theorem for structured IPs with a randomised experiment on unstructured ones showing the factor blowing up (pp. 7-8).
coauthors: Merve Bodur, Alberto Del Pia, Marco Molinaro, Sebastian Pokutta

quotes.text: Therefore, for these problems, in order to obtain cuts that are much stronger than original constraint cuts, one needs to consider more complicated cuts that cannot be generated through aggregations

From cut selection perspective, the insight here is that for packing and covering problems, using aggregation cuts may provide limited benefit over using cuts generated from only the original constraints, while aggregation cuts may produce significant value for general IPs.

title: Strong mixed-integer formulations for the floor layout problem
contribution: Uses the embedding approach systematically on the floor layout problem to recover all existing MIP formulations, derive new ones (including a refined unary formulation) and translatable valid inequalities, and solves previously unsolved benchmark instances in a public library.
problem_entry: Floor layout has many seemingly ad hoc MIP formulations and stays very hard; used as a case study in systematic formulation construction (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Vary encoding, disjunction and ground-set constraints in Vielma's embedding approach; ideal formulation for a small substructure; refined disjunction removing multiply-covered layouts; translate inequalities between encodings; glue pairwise formulations (pp. 6-16).
assumptions: Fixed rectangular floor, fixed box areas, bounded aspect ratio; area constraints are second-order-cone, linearised by CPLEX (pp. 1, 3, 19).
proof_devices: Ideal formulation for substructure Q^lb under lb_i + lb_j < L (Theorem 5.1; proof in Appendix B not read), pp. 10-11
Inequality translation between encodings (Prop. 6.1), pp. 14-15
Pairwise-to-N-box gluing (Prop. 7.1), p. 16
experiments: 11 literature instances, none previously solved, expanded to 99 by aspect ratio and noise; four formulations x four inequality levels; CPLEX 12.6 via JuMP, 4 h; Gurobi tried and dropped; root gaps, node trajectories, solve times; new techniques best on 55 of 99; code and instances on GitHub (pp. 17-23).
positioning: Unifies Meller et al., Sherali et al., Castillo-Westerlund, sequence-pair formulations; positions against heuristic literature that cannot prove optimality (pp. 3-4).
writing: Numbered contribution list (case study, valid inequalities, computational study) on pp. 1-2; candid 'no single formulation seems to be dominant' (p. 2, p. 20).
limits_future: No dominant formulation; RU better in nodes but not clearly in time; memory errors on hardest instances; recommends trying SP and RU with inequality subsets (pp. 20-23).

method_links.note: Exact (ideal) formulation of a small recurring substructure, then pairwise gluing; MILP-internal, not an import into a nonlinear class.
States openly that no formulation dominates (weak link).

transferable: Treat a literature's formulations as outputs of one generator (encoding x disjunction x ground set); recovering all of them validates the generator, the unexplored settings give new ones (pp. 2, 6-7).
Refine a disjunction whose branches overlap into a logically equivalent one with exclusive branches, and measure the effect by node count before solve time (pp. 12, 19).
Build a test family by perturbing base instances with controlled noise levels and shape parameters (p. 18).

quotes.text: While the construction approach focuses on the FLP, it also exemplifies generic formulation techniques that should prove useful for broader classes of problems.

We observe that, although there is no clearly superior formulation or approach across all benchmark instances, it is often the case that one approach will be the clear choice for a particular instance or family of instances.
